newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FEATURE - At 100, Bulgarian circus wants to be taken seriously.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - At 100, Bulgarian circus wants to be taken seriously.

text.p: Democracy has not been kind to the Bulgarian circus, one of the rare private enterprises to blossom under communist rule.
The circus, famed for the skill of its acrobats, marks its centenary this year in the same economic crisis affecting the rest of the country.
Promising young recruits no longer train at the Moscow Circus school, and many former acrobats have turned their muscles to the service of Bulgaria's criminal gangs.
The circus menagerie has shrunk to a few horses and ponies and one small lion.
But the artistes remain proud of the skills they have passed down the generations within circus families. The Waldemar and Palazov families have reached their seventh generation of performers.

"I am always annoyed when someone calls our parliament a circus, because circus art demands serious work and I wish our politicians had the commitment of circus artists as then the country would not have been in this state," said Bulgarian magician Orphy.
Last year there were five circuses operating in Bulgaria, three state-run and two private. This year, Georgi Kounov, head of the Bulgarian Circus Directorate, expects there to be fewer.

"Bulgarian artistes have created no new acts in the past seven years," said Todor Pironkov, artistic director of the Dobrich circus. As in the past, many Bulgarian performers work with circuses abroad.
REMEMBERING THE GOLDEN AGE
Acrobat Krustyu Parvanov said the golden age of the Bulgarian circus had been in the 1960s and 1970s.
"In those days there was tough competition between acrobats," he said. "There used to be 11 acrobatic troupes of 11 or 12 people each."
The Parvanovi won the prestigious Golden Clown award at the International Circus Festival in Monte Carlo in 1980.

Parvanov said circus performers had been able to travel freely to the West under communist rule. "Even in the old days, the National Intelligence Service never interrogated us, they never asked us what we did in the West," he said. "Perhaps they thought we were too stupid to get up to anything."
He said he believed the decline began when the Sofia State Circus big top burned down in September 1983. Then in 1992, the government removed the artistes' state employee status.
"All those young people had to find a way to make a living," Parvanov said. "As acrobats are quite strong, I'm sorry to say some went into shady insurance companies or became bodyguards."

The first Bulgarian circus performance took place at Easter 1897 in Sofia, organised by Petar Panayotov who modelled it on the visiting German, Austrian and Italian circus troupes which were travelling across the country.

The circus was nationalised after 1948 but is proud to have never received a state subsidy. As state employees, performers received a salary and travel allowances, but the circus made annual payments of about $200,000 to the culture ministry.

Conoisseurs of communist-era slogans recall with affection one at the former big top site which is said to have read -- with no irony intended -- "35 years of peoples' power in Bulgaria, 35 years of circus".
BLEAK FUTURE
Performers got together for a gala centenary weekend earlier this month at the circus's temporary site in a field next to Sofia's National Place of Culture, but the immediate future looks bleak.
Kounov dreams of renovating the dilapidated training area on the outskirts of Sofia, and of setting up a circus class at the Bulgarian choreography school.
Parvanov's father was a gymnast, who wore a mask for circus performances so that his respectable doctor father would not recognise him.

Parvanov joined the circus when the communist authorities would not let him study industrial chemistry. His son followed him, and now he says he would love to revive his award-winning troupe with his 12-year-old granddaughter. "She's very strong and flexible," he said. "You see, it's in the blood."
